bills.title: Sunshine Protection Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To make daylight savings time permanent, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Under current federal law, clocks in places that observe the change are set forward one hour on the second Sunday of March and back on the first Sunday of November. This bill ends that seasonal change by repealing the law that requires it, and instead moves all nine U.S. standard time zones permanently one hour later, so the later clock setting used during that period becomes the year-round standard.
bills.brief: Repeals the federal seasonal one-hour clock change and permanently shifts all nine U.S. standard time zones one hour later.

top_lines.headline: What Federal Time Law Does Now
subs: One-hour advance runs second Sunday of March to first Sunday of November
A State lying entirely in one zone may exempt itself by law
Nine zones set as offsets from Coordinated Universal Time

top_lines.headline: Permanent Shift to Later Clock Time
subs: Repeals the section that requires the seasonal one-hour advance
First zone moves from four to three hours behind Coordinated Universal Time
Ninth zone moves from ten to eleven hours ahead

top_lines.headline: Choice for States Already Exempt
subs: Exempt States and areas may keep their day-before-enactment clock
Choice is made as the State considers appropriate
No deadline, form, or filing step is stated

bills.likelihoodReason: A Republican-sponsored bill with 34 cosponsors, 31 of them Republicans, that carried the House 308-117 on Roll 238 under a closed rule and now sits with the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee per the latest-action record. The margin is far wider than the party split, which is the strongest structural signal in its favor; the Senate is Republican-majority and the sponsor's party controls the calendar. The counterweight is that the bill sets no effective date and repeals the exemption authority that States currently use, so any Senator whose State is exempt or wants a different permanent setting has a concrete drafting objection to raise rather than a purely political one.

sections.label: Section 2 — Making Daylight Savings Time Permanent

items.main: Section 2(a) repeals section 3 of the Uniform Time Act of 1966 (15 U.S.C. 260a) in full, ending the requirement that standard time be advanced one hour between the second Sunday of March and the first Sunday of November each year.
items.detail: The repealed section is the source of three separate rules, not one. Subsection (a) sets the seasonal advance and lets a State lying entirely within one time zone exempt itself by law, but only if that law makes the entire State including all its political subdivisions observe the otherwise-applicable standard time, and lets a State split across zones exempt either the whole State on those terms or the entire area of the State lying within one zone. Subsection (b) declares the express intent of Congress to supersede State and local laws that provide for different advances in time or changeover dates. Subsection (c) lets the Secretary of Transportation apply to a United States district court to enforce the section by injunction.

items.main: Section 2(b)(1) rewrites the second sentence of 15 U.S.C. 261(a) zone by zone, moving each of the nine standard time zones one hour later on a permanent basis.
items.detail: The first zone changes from Coordinated Universal Time retarded by 4 hours to 3 hours, the second from 5 to 4, the third from 6 to 5, the fourth from 7 to 6, the fifth from 8 to 7, the sixth from 9 to 8, the seventh from 10 to 9, and the eighth from 11 to 10. The ninth zone, which is stated as Coordinated Universal Time advanced rather than retarded, moves from advanced by 10 hours to advanced by 11 hours. The limits of each zone continue to be defined by order of the Secretary of Transportation, which the bill does not change.

items.main: Section 2(b)(2) adds a new 15 U.S.C. 261(b) letting a State, or an area of a State, that had exempted itself from the seasonal advance as of the day before enactment choose between the new standard time and the standard time that applied the day before enactment.
items.detail: The choice is stated as being made as the State considers appropriate, with no deadline, filing step, or procedure attached. The existing subsection (b), which defines Coordinated Universal Time as the scale maintained through the General Conference of Weights and Measures and interpreted or modified for the United States by the Secretary of Commerce in coordination with the Secretary of the Navy, is redesignated as subsection (c). Section 2(b)(3) then repoints the exception clause opening the second sentence of subsection (a) away from the repealed seasonal-advance section and toward the new subsection (b).

underreported.summary: Repealing 15 U.S.C. 260a removes more than the seasonal clock change. It also removes subsection (b), the express statement that Congress intends to supersede any State or local law providing for different advances in time or changeover dates, and subsection (c), the Secretary of Transportation's route to a district court injunction against violations.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned Repeal of Temporary Period for Daylight Savings Time and the repeal text is a single sentence, but the section being repealed carries three subsections; the preemption declaration and the enforcement mechanism go with it.

underreported.summary: The new state-election right in 15 U.S.C. 261(b) reaches only a State or area that had already exempted itself under 15 U.S.C. 260a(a) as in effect the day before enactment. Because section 2(a) repeals that exemption authority, the set of States and areas eligible to make the election is fixed at the moment of enactment.
underreported.why_unreported: The subsection reads as a general State option, but its operative trigger is a status held on a single past date under a section the same bill repeals.

criticisms.why: I rise in opposition to the bill and the danger it poses to our health and safety. This bill, sadly, is being rushed to the floor as a political bargaining chip without thorough consideration of the impacts, and we have been here before. Permanent time is a national decision with implications for every aspect of our health and economy. It deserves a robust, thoughtful debate and an amendment process that allows Members to test each provision of the bill.

gaps: The bill makes the later clock setting permanent but contains no effective-date provision, so the text does not state when the new zone offsets begin to apply.

The bill gives States and areas that were exempt the day before enactment a choice of standard time, but because it repeals the exemption authority in 15 U.S.C. 260a it provides no route for any other State to make that choice afterward.

The bill repeals the subsection declaring that Congress supersedes State and local laws providing for different advances in time or changeover dates, but does not state what happens to such State laws once that declaration is gone.

The new subsection (b) lets an exempt State pick its standard time as the State considers appropriate, but sets no deadline, no form of election, no notice to any federal officer, and no rule for changing the choice later.

Section 2(a) removes the Secretary of Transportation's district-court enforcement route for time violations without replacing it, while 15 U.S.C. 261(a) continues to leave the limits of each zone to that Secretary's order.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Pallone
featured_quotes.text: I rise today in strong support of the Sunshine Protection Act. This act addresses an issue on which many Americans actually agree, and that is stopping the biannual process of changing our clocks. Only 12 percent of Americans prefer to switch their clocks twice a year. Far more Americans recognize that the practice is inconvenient and, frankly, disruptive.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Cammack
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, today, I rise in strong support for H.R. 139, the Sunshine Protection Act, introduced by my friend and fellow Floridian, Congressman Vern Buchanan. This is one of those issues that has been highlighted here today that brings us together as Americans, regardless of party, no matter where you are. Everyone always asks the same question every year because we are all equally annoyed: Why in the heck are we still changing our clocks?

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Guthrie
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate my friend from Florida yielding. It is fun today because I have my friend from Florida controlling time. I  have another friend from Florida (Mr. Soto) speaking for the bill, and we have the sponsor from Florida. I will say also to the American people, Mr. Speaker, through you, that a very famous resident of Florida mentioned this to me in the Oval Office a few weeks ago, so I know there is strong support. It is actually called the Sunshine Protection Act, and the reason is people like the longer daylight hours.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Carter
featured_quotes.text: Twice a year, Americans lose sleep, disrupt their routines, and pay the price for a practice that has outlived its original purpose. H.R. 139, the Sunshine Protection Act, ends that twice-yearly clock change and makes daylight saving time permanent year round. Research shows that eliminating the biannual switch reduces the spike in heart attacks, strokes, and workplace accidents that follow the spring-forward transition. Ending the clock change also means fewer disruptions to sleep patterns tied to that adjustment period.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steube
featured_quotes.text: For me, this vote has been nearly a decade in the making. In 2018, at the Braden River Barber Shop shortly after we turned back the clocks to standard time, everyone was complaining about the change. Kids are not waking up on time. Everyone is tired. There is a rise in health-related issues. Nobody is able to enjoy activities in the evening. The list went on and on. The question was: Why are we still changing the clocks? As a State senator in Florida at the time, everyone looked at me and asked if we could do something about it, so we did.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Sessions
featured_quotes.text: My dear friend, the gentleman from Florida, Vern Buchanan, years ago began this process, understanding that it was more than just an issue that Congress would deal with. It is also an issue that is called spring forward, fall back. You fall back as we get to October, and that means you lose the time, the light that you had all this time.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Dean
featured_quotes.text: I rise in opposition to the bill and the danger it poses to our health and safety. This bill, sadly, is being rushed to the floor as a political bargaining chip without thorough consideration of the impacts, and we have been here before. Permanent time is a national decision with implications for every aspect of our health and economy. It deserves a robust, thoughtful debate and an amendment process that allows Members to test each provision of the bill.

added: A new 15 U.S.C. 261(b) letting a State, or an exempted area of a State, that was exempt from the seasonal advance on the day before enactment choose between the new standard time and the standard time in effect that day
modified: 15 U.S.C. 261(a): first zone moves from Coordinated Universal Time retarded by 4 hours to 3 hours, second from 5 to 4, third from 6 to 5, fourth from 7 to 6, fifth from 8 to 7, sixth from 9 to 8, seventh from 10 to 9, eighth from 11 to 10
15 U.S.C. 261(a): ninth zone moves from Coordinated Universal Time advanced by 10 hours to advanced by 11 hours
15 U.S.C. 261: the existing subsection (b) defining Coordinated Universal Time is redesignated as subsection (c)
15 U.S.C. 261(a): the exception clause opening the second sentence is repointed from the repealed seasonal-advance section to the new state-election subsection
removed: 15 U.S.C. 260a in full: the one-hour advance from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November, the State and area exemption from it, the express supersession of State and local laws providing different advances in time or changeover dates, and the Secretary of Transportation's district-court enforcement route
